429: For a finite list of actions, the general selector and measurability
430: requirements have a concrete implementation: evaluate the scores and choose
431: the first maximizer in a fixed ordering.  The following corollary records
432: the precise version used by finite-action policies.
433: 
434: \begin{corollary}[Measurably enumerated finite domains]
435: \label{cor:finite-enumeration-new}
436: Suppose there is a positive $\cHist_t^-$-measurable integer $K_t$ and
437: $\cHist_t^-$-measurable actions $a_{t,k}:\Omega\to\mathsf A$, $k\ge1$, such
438: that
439: \[
440:  \cA_t=\{a_{t,1},\ldots,a_{t,K_t}\}.
441: \]
442: If the learner chooses the smallest index attaining the score maximum, then the
443: selected action is $\cHist_t$-measurable and
444: \eqref{eq:approx-score-oracle-new} holds with $\xi_t=0$.  The score and
445: mean-reward suprema and the universal actionwise events reduce to measurable
446: finite maxima and intersections.  A fixed finite action set is the immediate
447: special case.
448: \end{corollary}
449: 
450: \paragraph{The order of a decision round.}
451: Algorithm~\ref{alg:transported-ucb} uses the corrected center constructed in
452: \Cref{sec:corrected-center}.  The learner forms and certifies its scores
453: before seeing the reward, selects an action, and only then updates the frozen
454: statistics.  This timing keeps the collection-time queries eligible for the
455: sequential confidence argument.  Selection and the regret analysis must use
456: the same computed width map, as the remark above emphasizes.
457: 
458: \begin{algorithm}[t]
459: \caption{Corrected-center specialization of transported UCB}\label{alg:transported-ucb}
460: \begin{algorithmic}[1]
461: \STATE Observe the context and graph-measurable action correspondence $\cA_t$; this defines $\cHist_t^-$.
462: \STATE Take the prefix-determined $\btheta_t$, $\bVbar_t$, and $\bV_t$; using the observed context, form $\bq_t(a)$, $m_t^{\rm corr}(a)$, and $b_t(a)$.
463: \STATE Choose $\cHist_t^-$-measurable failure budgets before their corresponding draws; reveal the pre-reward randomness $\Omega_t$.
464: \STATE Construct $\Calg_t$ and obtain pre-reward certificates $\bar D_t$, $\kappa_{-,t}$, and $\kappa_{+,t}$.
465: \STATE Obtain one jointly measurable solver upper-width map $\hat s_t(a)$ over the score domain.
466: \STATE Return a $\cHist_t$-measurable $\xi_t$-approximate selector for the score in \eqref{eq:transported-score-new}.
467: \STATE Observe the reward; update the frozen ridge estimator and \eqref{eq:reference-update-new}.
468: \end{algorithmic}
469: \end{algorithm}
470: 
471: The algorithm leaves the linear algebra implementation open.  Exact Cholesky
472: solves satisfy the solver conditions in exact arithmetic.  Conjugate gradient
473: (CG) can instead solve each action system using products with a fixed SPD
474: operator; a residual or energy argument must certify its returned widths.
475: Changing the matrix through a window, subsample, or sketch is a separate
476: approximation and requires an operator comparison.  The controlled experiment
477: in \Cref{sec:transport-followup} uses dense exact-current matrices and
478: Cholesky solves, so it does not evaluate these approximate or matrix-free paths.
479: 
480: \section{How to compare the frozen and current matrices}
481: \label{sec:logarithmic-transport}
482: 
483: The main theorem assumes a comparison between matrices.  This section explains
484: how to obtain one when past gradients are recomputed at the current parameter.
485: The matrix order $A\preceq B$ means that $B-A$ is positive semidefinite: the
486: quadratic form of $B$ is at least that of $A$ in every direction.  A two-sided
487: comparison therefore controls all query widths at once.
488: 
489: \paragraph{Measure relative change along a path.}
490: Imagine continuously changing the frozen matrix into the current matrix.
491: The path-length integrand below measures the largest relative change at each
492: point, after normalizing by the matrix there.  Integrating those changes gives
493: a multiplicative comparison between the endpoints.  The exponential form
494: allows large changes; it does not promise that the resulting factor is small.
495: 
496: \begin{lemma}[Logarithmic comparison along an SPD path]
497: \label{lem:log-spd-path}
498: Let $\bV:[0,1]\to\mathbb{S}_{++}^d$ be entrywise absolutely continuous and
499: let $\dot\bV(\tau)$ denote its almost-everywhere derivative.  If
500: \begin{equation}\label{eq:generic-path-length-new}
501:  \mathcal D(\bV)=\int_0^1
502:  \|\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\dot\bV(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}\,d\tau,
503: \end{equation}
504: then
505: \begin{equation}\label{eq:log-path-sandwich-new}
506:  e^{-\mathcal D(\bV)}\bV(0)\preceq\bV(1)
507:  \preceq e^{\mathcal D(\bV)}\bV(0).
508: \end{equation}
509: No commutativity or small-path assumption is required.
510: \end{lemma}
511: 
512: \begin{remark}[Thompson distance and selected-path length]
513: The integrand in \eqref{eq:generic-path-length-new} is the classical Thompson
514: Finsler norm on the positive-definite cone
515: \citep{thompson1963certain,nussbaum1994finsler}.  Its endpoint metric is
516: \[
517:  d_{\rm Th}(A,B)
518:  :=\inf\{r\ge0:e^{-r}A\preceq B\preceq e^rA\}.
519: \]
520: Equivalently,
521: \[
522:  d_{\rm Th}(A,B)
523:  =\left\|\log(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\right\|_{\rm op}.
524: \]
525: Therefore \Cref{lem:log-spd-path} gives
526: \begin{align*}
527:  d_{\rm Th}(\bV(0),\bV(1))&\le\mathcal D(\bV),\\
528:  d_{\rm Th}(\bVbar_t,\bV_t)&\le\mathcal D_t\le\bar D_t.
529: \end{align*}
530: The endpoint distance depends only on the two metrics, whereas
531: $\mathcal D(\bV)$ depends on the selected path.  The direct SPD path length is
532: independent of a factorization; the upper bound from
533: \Cref{lem:factor-spd-path} depends on the chosen factorization and interpolation.
534: \end{remark}
535: 
536: \begin{remark}[Sharpness of the symmetric exponential factors]
537: For $D\ge0$, let
538: \[
539: \begin{aligned}
540:  \bVbar&=\bI_2,&
541:  \bV&=\begin{pmatrix}e^D&0\\0&e^{-D}\end{pmatrix},\\
542:  \bV(\tau)&=\begin{pmatrix}e^{D\tau}&0\\0&e^{-D\tau}\end{pmatrix}.
543: \end{aligned}
544: \]
545: Then
546: \[
547:  \bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\dot\bV(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}
548:  =\begin{pmatrix}D&0\\0&-D\end{pmatrix},
549: \]
550: so $\mathcal D(\bV)=d_{\rm Th}(\bVbar,\bV)=D$.  For $q_1=e_1$,
551: $\bar s(q_1)=1$ and $s(q_1)=e^{-D/2}$, so
552: $\bar s=e^{D/2}s$ is attained.  For $q_2=e_2$,
553: $s(q_2)=e^{D/2}$ and $\bar s(q_2)=1$, so
554: $s=e^{D/2}\bar s$ is attained.  Thus each one-way factor is sharp, and a
555: uniform argument based only on the symmetric Thompson-distance bound cannot
556: improve the resulting round-trip factor $e^D$.  This is a metric-factor
557: sharpness statement, not a contextual-bandit regret lower bound and not a
558: claim that every trajectory attains the worst case.
559: \end{remark}
560: 
561: \paragraph{Work with the gradients that form the matrix.}
562: A replay matrix is a ridge term plus a Gram matrix of gradient features.
563: Stack those features as rows of $\Bmat$.  It is often easier to bound how
564: these rows change than to analyze the full SPD path directly.  The next lemma
565: turns a bound on the changing factor into a bound on matrix path length.
566: Its normalization by $\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}$ retains information about which
567: directions the data have already constrained.
568: 
569: \begin{lemma}[Rectangular factor-path certificate]
570: \label{lem:factor-spd-path}
571: Let $\Bmat:[0,1]\to\R^{m\times d}$ be absolutely continuous and set
572: $\bV(\tau)=\lambda\bI+\Bmat(\tau)^\top\Bmat(\tau)$, with $\lambda>0$.
573: Then
574: \begin{equation}\label{eq:factor-path-bound-new}
575:  \mathcal D(\bV)\le2\int_0^1
576:  \|\dot\Bmat(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}\,d\tau.
577: \end{equation}
578: More generally, suppose there is a measurable function
579: $\nu_t:[0,1]\to[0,\infty)$ with $\nu_t\in L^1([0,1])$ such that
580: \[
581:  \dot\Bmat(\tau)^\top\dot\Bmat(\tau)
582:  \preceq\nu_t(\tau)^2\bV(\tau)
583: \]
584: almost everywhere.  Then
585: $\mathcal D(\bV)\le2\int_0^1\nu_t(\tau)d\tau$.  For nonnegative $\nu_t$, the
586: displayed PSD premise is equivalently the norm condition
587: $\|\dot\Bmat(\tau)\bV(\tau)^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}\le\nu_t(\tau)$ almost everywhere.
588: \end{lemma}
589: 
590: For a scalar prediction, each past observation contributes a gradient row.
591: Move that row from its collection-time parameter $\btheta_s$ to the current
592: parameter $\btheta_t$ along its own straight segment.  The $s$th row is
593: \begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-factor-path-new}
594:  \sigma^{-1}\nabla_\theta\mu_{\btheta_s+
595:  \tau(\btheta_t-\btheta_s)}(x_s,a_s)^\top.
596: \end{equation}
597: The endpoint matrices are the frozen and exact current matrices.  The path
598: between them is a device for comparing those endpoints: different rows begin
599: at different collection-time parameters.  It need not be the generalized
600: Gauss--Newton (GGN) matrix of any common intermediate model, and it is not the
601: learner's training trajectory.
602: A weighted or heteroscedastic squared loss uses row
603: $\sqrt{w_s}\,\nabla\mu^\top$ for a nonnegative collection-time weight $w_s$
604: fixed before the corresponding reward.
605: If the weight is fixed along the interpolation, the same proof only rescales
606: the corresponding row.  If it changes with the path, the derivative of
607: $\sqrt{w_s(\tau)}$ is an additional obligation.
608: 
609: \paragraph{A certificate from smoothness and parameter movement.}
610: A prediction-Hessian bound controls how fast each gradient can change along
611: its segment.  Combined with the ridge lower bound on the matrix, it gives a
612: certificate in terms of $Q_t$, the accumulated squared distances from the
613: current parameter to collection-time parameters.  This route is easy to state,
614: but it can discard information about well-constrained directions.
615: 
616: \begin{corollary}[Hessian path certificate]
617: \label{cor:hessian-path-new}
618: Suppose the parameter region is convex and
619: $\|\nabla_\theta^2\mu_\theta(x_s,a_s)\|_{\rm op}\le L_g$ along every segment
620: in \eqref{eq:scalar-factor-path-new}.  With
621: \begin{equation}\label{eq:Qt-new}
622:  Q_t=\sum_{s<t}\|\btheta_t-\btheta_s\|_2^2,
623: \end{equation}
624: the exact current and frozen metrics satisfy
625: \begin{equation}\label{eq:hessian-path-sandwich-new}
626:  e^{-\bar D_t}\bVbar_t\preceq\bV_t\preceq e^{\bar D_t}\bVbar_t,
627:  \qquad
628:  \bar D_t=\frac{2L_g\sqrt{Q_t}}{\sigma\sqrt\lambda}.
629: \end{equation}
630: This remains valid when $\bar D_t\ge1$.  At $t=1$, the factor has zero rows,
631: $Q_1=0$, and both metrics equal $\lambda\bI$.
632: \end{corollary}
633: 
634: The relative condition in \Cref{lem:factor-spd-path} retains that directional
635: information and can be much sharper than the ridge-only Hessian bound.
636: Changes in directions with larger matrix eigenvalues are downweighted by
637: the inverse-matrix normalization.  Both constructions permit gradient
638: rotation; the factor-path lemma requires neither a fixed subspace nor known
639: rank.
640: 
641: \paragraph{Convert matrix comparisons into width comparisons.}
642: The next proposition gives the outward and return comparisons used in the
643: regret theorem.  It also shows how a relative-error bound for an approximate
644: operator supplies the factors $\kappa_{-,t}$ and $\kappa_{+,t}$.
645: 
646: \begin{proposition}[Width transport and approximate operators]
647: \label{prop:width-transport-new}
648: Under \eqref{eq:path-length-new} and \eqref{eq:operator-sandwich-new},
649: \begin{align}
650:  \bar s_t^2(a)&\le e^{\bar D_t}\kappa_{+,t}s_{\Calg,t}^2(a),
651:  &s_{\Calg,t}^2(a)&\le
652:  e^{\bar D_t}\kappa_{-,t}^{-1}\bar s_t^2(a).
653:  \label{eq:two-way-width-new}
654: \end{align}
655: Exact current curvature has $\kappa_{-,t}=\kappa_{+,t}=1$.  More generally,
656: the operational relative-error certificate
657: \begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-operator-certificate-new}
658:  \|\bV_t^{-1/2}(\Calg_t-\bV_t)\bV_t^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}
659:  \le\varepsilon_t<1
660: \end{equation}
661: gives $\kappa_{-,t}=1-\varepsilon_t$ and
662: $\kappa_{+,t}=1+\varepsilon_t$.  An upper comparison alone does not imply a
663: lower factor.
664: \end{proposition}
665: 
666: \paragraph{Compare the endpoints directly when possible.}
667: Following an entire path is not required if a valid two-sided comparison of
668: the endpoint matrices is already available.  The next corollary inserts that
669: comparison into the same confidence and regret argument.  Its upper factor
670: protects optimism; its lower factor supplies the return comparison, so their
671: ratio enters the regret bound.
672: 
673: \begin{corollary}[Direct endpoint sandwich]
674: \label{cor:relative-endpoint-ucb}
675: Replace the path premise \eqref{eq:path-length-new} in
676: \Cref{thm:transported-ucb} by pre-reward measurable factors that, on the joint
677: certificate event, satisfy
678: \begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-endpoint-sandwich}
679:  0<c_{-,t}\le c_{+,t}<\infty,\qquad
680:  c_{-,t}\bVbar_t\preceq\bV_t\preceq c_{+,t}\bVbar_t.
681: \end{equation}
682: Replace \eqref{eq:transported-score-new} by the score
683: \begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-endpoint-score}
684:  U_t^{\rm rel}(a)=m_t(a)+\beta_t\sqrt{c_{+,t}\kappa_{+,t}}
685:  \hat s_t(a)+b_t(a),
686: \end{equation}
687: and require the same finite measurable supremum and approximate-selector
688: condition for this score.  Keep every other hypothesis of that theorem.
689: On the joint confidence and certificate event, writing
690: $h_t=1+\alpha_t\sqrt{c_{+,t}\kappa_{+,t}/(c_{-,t}\kappa_{-,t})}$,
691: \begin{align}
692:  \operatorname{reg}_t
693:  &\le\beta_t h_t\bar s_t(a_t)+2b_t(a_t)+\xi_t,\nonumber\\
694:  R_T&\le\sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)
695:  \gamma_T\sum_{t=1}^T\beta_t^2h_t^2}
696:  +2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t.
697:  \label{eq:relative-endpoint-regret}
698: \end{align}
699: The probability statement of \Cref{thm:transported-ucb} is unchanged, with
700: the endpoint certificate included in its joint certificate event.
701: \end{corollary}
702: 
703: This result uses the endpoint matrices directly.  In particular,
704: $\max\{-\log c_{-,t},\log c_{+,t}\}$ bounds their Thompson distance;
705: it need not bound the length of the synthetic path
706: \eqref{eq:scalar-factor-path-new}.  Its effective width still obeys the
707: reference-width floor: $\sqrt{c_{+,t}\kappa_{+,t}}\hat s_t(a)\ge\bar s_t(a)$.
708: 
709: \paragraph{What extends to vector outputs?}
710: The factor construction also accommodates several output coordinates and
711: weights, provided their changes are controlled as well.  For vector outputs,
712: let $J_s(\theta)\in\R^{p_s\times d}$ and supply an
713: absolutely continuous factor $R_s(\theta)\in\R^{r_s\times p_s}$ satisfying
714: $R_s^\top R_s=W_s\succeq0$.  Stacking
715: $B_s=R_sJ_s\in\R^{r_s\times d}$ gives
716: $\lambda I+\sum_sJ_s^\top W_sJ_s$.  Along a path,
717: $\dot B_s=\dot R_sJ_s+R_s\dot J_s$; both terms must be controlled.  This
718: covers the geometry of weighted Fisher/GGN factors but does not by itself prove
719: a likelihood confidence sequence or an exponential-family regret theorem.
720: 
721: \section{A confidence center that does not require optimizer convergence}
722: \label{sec:corrected-center}
723: 
724: So far, the confidence band has been an assumption.  We now construct one
725: for squared loss.  The difficulty is that an arbitrarily trained nonlinear
726: predictor need not be the center of a valid confidence band.  The construction
727: uses that predictor as an anchor, then corrects it using a linear estimate
728: formed from collection-time features.  Confidence comes from this frozen
729: linear estimation problem; it does not require the nonlinear optimizer to
730: have converged.
731: 
732: There is a cost to this separation.  Linearizing the model introduces Taylor
733: error, and the reference model may not exactly represent the true mean.
734: The resulting band must account for both errors, in past observations and in
735: the current prediction.  The assumptions below make these costs explicit.
736: 
737: \paragraph{Noise and the reference model.}
738: Let $\sigma>0$ and let the reward obey
739: $r_t=\mu_t^*(a_t)+\eta_t$, where, for every $u\in\R$,
740: \begin{equation}\label{eq:new-noise-condition}
741:  \mathbb E[\exp(u\eta_t)\mid\cHist_t]
742:  \le\exp(u^2\sigma^2/2).
743: \end{equation}
744: Thus the noise condition is imposed after the action is selected and before
745: the reward is revealed.  The ridge penalty is centered at zero in the chosen
746: parameter coordinates, and every norm bound below, including
747: $\|\btheta^\circ\|_2\le S$, uses those coordinates.  For a pretrained
748: initialization $\btheta_0$, the intended convention is displacement coordinates
749: $\btheta=\btheta_{\rm orig}-\btheta_0$; then $S$ bounds the displacement of the
750: reference model from initialization rather than its raw parameter norm.  Fix
751: before data collection a reference parameter $\btheta^\circ\in\Theta$ with
752: $\|\btheta^\circ\|_2\le S$, and allow
753: approximate realizability
754: \begin{equation}\label{eq:approx-realizability-new}
755:  \mu^*(z)=\mu_{\btheta^\circ}(z)+m^\circ(z),\qquad
756:  |m^\circ(z)|\le\epsilon_{\rm mis}(z).
757: \end{equation}
758: \paragraph{Turn past rewards into a frozen linear estimation problem.}
759: The predictable sequence $\btheta_t\in\Theta$ is otherwise arbitrary.  Set
760: $\bq_t(a)=\nabla_\theta\mu_{\btheta_t}(x_t,a)$.  A collection-time
761: linearization has a known nonlinear offset and a linear term in the reference
762: parameter.  Subtracting that offset from the reward gives a
763: \emph{pseudo-response}: an approximate linear observation of the fixed
764: reference parameter, with noise and Taylor and misspecification errors.
765: The pseudo-responses and their frozen ridge estimate are
766: \begin{align}
767:  y_s&=r_s-\mu_{\btheta_s}(x_s,a_s)+\bq_s(a_s)^\top\btheta_s,
768:  \label{eq:pseudo-response-new}\\
769:  \hat\btheta_t^{\rm lin}
770:  &=\bVbar_t^{-1}\sigma^{-2}\sum_{s<t}\bq_s(a_s)y_s.
771:  \label{eq:frozen-ridge-new}
772: \end{align}
773: \paragraph{Correct the current prediction.}
774: The linear estimate uses old, predictable features, while the action query
775: uses the current model.  The corrected center connects them:
776: \begin{equation}\label{eq:corrected-center-new}
777:  m_t^{\rm corr}(a)=\mu_{\btheta_t}(x_t,a)
778:  +\bq_t(a)^\top(\hat\btheta_t^{\rm lin}-\btheta_t).
779: \end{equation}
780: 
781: The correction applies the current gradient to the difference between the
782: frozen linear estimate and the current parameter.  Thus the certified center
783: is generally different from the raw prediction of the trained model.  The
784: identity supporting its confidence band holds for any predictable parameter
785: path in the certified region, but it does not make the approximation errors
786: small.
787: 
788: \paragraph{Account for historical and current errors separately.}
789: Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$.  Let $\rho_s^\circ$ be the Taylor remainder of
790: $\mu_{\btheta^\circ}$ around $\btheta_s$, and supply envelopes
791: \begin{equation}\label{eq:lin-mis-envelopes-new}
792:  |\rho_s^\circ|\le\epsilon_{\rm lin}(s),\qquad
793:  |m^\circ(x_s,a_s)|\le\epsilon_{\rm mis}(s),
794: \end{equation}
795: with the corresponding actionwise current envelopes
796: $\epsilon_{\rm lin,t}(a)$ and $\epsilon_{\rm mis,t}(a)$.  Each envelope is
797: deterministic or measurable before the reward at the round where it is used;
798: the complete historical sum below is known before selecting $a_t$.
799: Past errors affect the fitted linear estimate and therefore enlarge the
800: confidence radius.  Current errors enter the final prediction band
